text: We built scheduling software for dental clinics. Three clinics love it and use it every day, but every other clinic I demo to says it looks nice and they'll think about it. I can't tell if we're stuck selling to enthusiasts or if the product is just wrong. How do I get from these 3 happy customers to the next 50?

We went from 8 to 35 people in six months. Decisions I used to make in five minutes now sit waiting on me for days, and two of my best engineers just quit saying they feel stuck. I know I'm the bottleneck. I don't know what to hand off first or how.

A big incumbent just shipped a free version of our main feature. We're at $18k MRR and flat for three months. Do I double down, narrow to a niche they won't bother with, or pivot? I need a way to think about this that isn't panic.

I've worked on my startup idea nights and weekends for eight months. I still haven't quit my job or shown it to a single customer. Every time I get close to launching I find another thing to fix. I think I'm scared of finding out it doesn't work.

A client we'd chased for two years just rejected us and it wrecked me for two weeks. My cofounder bounced back in a day. I keep replaying it and I'm making worse decisions because of it. How do I stop spiralling when something big fails?

A seed investor offered $1.2M at an $8M post-money but wants a 2x liquidation preference and a board seat. Another one says maybe in two months. I have five months of runway. Do I take the offer or wait?

I make $140k at a startup and I'm thinking of leaving to build my own thing. We have $60k saved and a mortgage, and my wife is nervous. How should I think about how much risk with my own money is sane before I quit?

I'm pitching twelve investors next week. My deck is 28 slides, and last time investors were checking their phones by slide six. I freeze when someone interrupts me. How do I take control of the room and not just present at it?

My biggest customer is 40% of revenue and wants a 30% discount at renewal or they'll leave. I don't think they will, but I can't risk it. How do I negotiate this without getting steamrolled or burning the relationship?
Our landing page says 'AI-powered workflow automation platform' and nobody remembers us. People nod on calls and then forget. How do I explain what we do so that it sticks and gets repeated?

We have to decide in two weeks whether to build the enterprise feature our one big prospect asked for or stay focused on self-serve. The team is split 50/50 and I keep flip-flopping. How do I decide without just going with my gut or with whoever argues loudest?
My financial model says we hit $1M ARR in 14 months. Last year's model was off by 3x. I'm about to hire against this forecast. How do I forecast in a way I can actually trust?

We have 11 months of runway and one customer is 60% of revenue. If they leave we're dead. Everyone says diversify, but I want to understand what a company that survives a shock like that actually looks like.

I run a six-person agency doing content and support for ecommerce brands. AI tools are eating our margin every month. Do I become an AI-enabled service, build a product, or get out while we're still profitable?
I want to build software for AI agents in healthcare billing. Everyone tells me it's early. How do I know whether I'm too early or whether the market will be there by the time we're ready?
We're a project management tool in a crowded space. Our investors keep saying 'create a category'. I don't know what that means in practice for a four-person company with no brand.

I need to hire my first head of sales. I've never managed sales and I'm afraid of picking the wrong person or being fooled by a great interview. How do I evaluate candidates and then set them up to succeed?

My cofounder and I have stopped talking about anything except tasks. I think he resents that I took the CEO title. Every disagreement feels personal now. How do I fix this before it breaks the company?
I need our best advisor to open five investor intros for us but he's busy and replies to nothing. How do I ask in a way that he'll actually say yes and follow through?

I charge $29 a month and have 400 customers who rarely complain. A friend says I'm badly underpriced. If I double the price I'm scared I'll lose half of them. How do I find the right price without gambling the business?
